title: Noetherian descent along an injective finite ring extension
statement: Let $i:B\to A$ be an injective homomorphism of commutative rings. Suppose $A$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and is a finitely generated $B$-module via $i$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Then $B$ is Noetherian.

source.document: P. M. Eakin, Jr., The converse to a well known theorem on Noetherian rings, Math. Ann. 177 (1968), 278–282 (WANTED; not in literature/)
source.place: Main theorem (finite extension converse); needed for the Noetherian quotient base in ILO Exposé VI, paragraph after Proposition 3.5.

proof.text: In this proof a module is Noetherian if every submodule is finitely generated, with finite generation as in [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. We will use the following elementary quotient observation. If $V$ is a Noetherian $R$-module and $U\subseteq V$, any submodule $L\subseteq V/U$ is the image of its inverse image in $V$; images of a finite generating family generate $L$. Thus $V/U$ is Noetherian. Submodules of $V$ are Noetherian because their submodules are also submodules of $V$. Finally, if an ideal $J$ annihilates $V$, the $R$-submodules and $R/J$-submodules coincide, and an $R$-linear combination depends only on coefficient classes in $R/J$; hence finite generation and Noetherianity over these two scalar rings coincide.

source.document: P. M. Eakin, Jr., The converse to a well known theorem on Noetherian rings, Math. Ann. 177 (1968), 278–282 (WANTED; not in literature/)
source.place: Agent-written finite-module proof of the main theorem, using the Formanek maximal-faithful-quotient argument (Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §3, Theorems 3.6–3.7; WANTED, not in literature/).

proof.text: Here is the finite evaluation observation used below. For a commutative ring $R$ and a finite faithful Noetherian $R$-module $V$, choose generators $v_1,\ldots,v_s$. Faithful means that $rv=0$ for every $v\in V$ implies $r=0$. The $R$-linear map $e:R\to V^s$, $r\mapsto(rv_1,\ldots,rv_s)$, is injective: if all coordinates vanish, $r$ kills every linear combination of the generators. By [lem-per-noetherian-module-finite-product], $V^s$ is Noetherian. For any ideal $H\subseteq R$, choose generators of the submodule $e(H)$ and lift them to $H$; injectivity shows that these lifts generate $H$. Therefore every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated, so $R$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. This also covers $s=0$, when faithfulness forces $R=0$.

source.document: P. M. Eakin, Jr., The converse to a well known theorem on Noetherian rings, Math. Ann. 177 (1968), 278–282 (WANTED; not in literature/)

proof.text: Regard $A$ as a finite $B$-module through $i$. We prove it is Noetherian as a $B$-module. Suppose it is not. For a $B$-ideal $I$ write $IA$ for the ideal generated in $A$ by $i(I)$. The set of ideals $IA$ for which $A/IA$ is not Noetherian as a $B$-module is nonempty, since $I=0$ belongs to it. Since $A$ is a Noetherian ring, [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-ideal-set-maximal] gives a maximal member $I_0A$ of this set. Set $M=A/I_0A$. Its generators are the images of a fixed finite $B$-generating family of $A$.

source.document: P. M. Eakin, Jr., The converse to a well known theorem on Noetherian rings, Math. Ann. 177 (1968), 278–282 (WANTED; not in literature/)
source.place: Agent-written finite-module proof of the main theorem, using the Formanek maximal-faithful-quotient argument (Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §3, Theorems 3.6–3.7; WANTED, not in literature/).

proof.text: Put $J=\{b\in B:i(b)A\subseteq I_0A\}$, the annihilator of $M$, and $R=B/J$. We have $I_0\subseteq J$ and $JA=I_0A$: one inclusion follows from $I_0\subseteq J$, the other from the defining condition on $J$. Thus $M$ is a finite faithful $R$-module and is not Noetherian, by Step 1. If $H\ne0$ is an ideal of $R$, its inverse image $L\subseteq B$ strictly contains $J$. Then $LA$ strictly contains $JA$: equality would imply $L\subseteq J$ by the definition of $J$. Maximality in Step 3 says that $A/LA$ is Noetherian over $B$. The quotient of $A$ by the inverse image of $HM$ is $A/LA$, since that inverse image is $LA+I_0A=LA$. Hence $M/HM$ is Noetherian over $R$ by Step 1, for every nonzero ideal $H$ of $R$.

source.place: Agent-written finite-module proof of the main theorem, using the Formanek maximal-faithful-quotient argument (Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §3, Theorems 3.6–3.7; WANTED, not in literature/).

proof.text: Consider the set $\mathcal S$ of $R$-submodules $N\subseteq M$ for which $M/N$ is faithful. It contains $0$. A nonempty chain has union $N_\infty$, an $R$-submodule. If $rM\subseteq N_\infty$, finitely many generators $m_1,\ldots,m_s$ of $M$ give finitely many elements $rm_j$ in that union. Choose one chain member containing all of them; when the family is empty choose any member of the nonempty chain. This member contains $rM$, so faithfulness of its quotient gives $r=0$. Thus $M/N_\infty$ is faithful. The empty chain has upper bound $0$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-zorn-lemma] to these underlying subsets of $M$, with the indicated chain upper bounds, to obtain a maximal $N_0\in\mathcal S$. Set $Q=M/N_0$. It is finite and faithful. By maximality, $Q/U$ is not faithful for every nonzero submodule $U\subseteq Q$: its inverse image in $M$ strictly contains $N_0$.

source.place: Agent-written finite-module proof of the main theorem, using the Formanek maximal-faithful-quotient argument (Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §3, Theorems 3.6–3.7; WANTED, not in literature/).

proof.text: If $Q$ were Noetherian, Step 2 would make $R$ Noetherian. Since $M$ is finite over $R$, [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite] would then make every submodule of $M$ finite, contrary to the choice of $M$. Thus $Q$ is not Noetherian. On the other hand, for every nonzero ideal $H\subseteq R$, the map $M\to Q$ induces a surjection $M/HM\to Q/HQ$; the image of $HM$ is exactly $HQ$, by writing elements as finite sums of scalar multiples. Step 4 and the quotient observation of Step 1 imply that $Q/HQ$ is Noetherian.

proof.text: Let $U\subseteq Q$ be a nonzero $R$-submodule. Since $Q/U$ is not faithful by Step 5, there is $0\ne a\in R$ with $aQ\subseteq U$. The module $aQ$ is finite: multiply a finite generating family of $Q$ by $a$. By Step 6, $Q/aQ$ is Noetherian (apply it to the nonzero principal ideal $(a)$), so its submodule $U/aQ$ has a finite generating family. Lift that family to $u_1,\ldots,u_t\in U$. Every $u\in U$ differs from an $R$-linear combination of the $u_j$ by an element of $aQ$; adjoining generators of $aQ$ therefore generates $U$. The zero submodule has the empty generating family. Every submodule of $Q$ is consequently finite, contradicting Step 6. This contradiction proves that the original $B$-module $A$ is Noetherian.

source.place: Agent-written finite-module proof of the main theorem, using the Formanek maximal-faithful-quotient argument (Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §3, Theorems 3.6–3.7; WANTED, not in literature/).

proof.text: For a $B$-ideal $H$, the subset $i(H)\subseteq A$ is a $B$-submodule, hence has finitely many $B$-module generators by the preceding conclusion. Lift these generators to $H$. Since $i$ is injective, they generate $H$: apply $i$ to any proposed linear combination and use injectivity on the difference. Thus every ideal of $B$ is finitely generated, which is exactly that $B$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. If $A=0$, injectivity forces $B=0$, and the same conclusion holds.
